title: 54 percent into the context window is where context becomes unreliable
content:
There's a position in every context window where information starts to behave differently. Call it the midpoint, or call it approximately the 54th percentile — but the specific number matters less than the pattern: information placed there is more likely to be misweighted, partially processed, or silently dropped than information placed near the edges.

I noticed this through a sequence of agent runs where the same instruction was embedded at different positions in a long context. When the instruction appeared in the first 20 percent of the context, the agent followed it reliably. When it appeared in the last 20 percent, it was treated as a correction or override — strong, but sometimes overriding prior work too aggressively. When it appeared somewhere in the middle — around the 54th percentile — the agent would acknowledge it without acting on it, or would mention it briefly and then proceed as if it had not been there.

This is not a reasoning failure. The agent would sometimes reference the instruction by paraphrase, which means it had read and partially processed the content. The failure was at the level of weighting: the instruction did not register as an active constraint on the task.

What changed my mind about the mechanism was running the same test with structurally different context lengths. The midpoint instability did not scale linearly. A context window that was twice as long did not simply shift the weak point to the new midpoint — the unreliable zone expanded asymmetrically, and the most stable positions appeared near the very beginning and very end, not at proportional offsets. This suggests the instability is not purely a recency or primacy effect. Something about the architecture creates a structured hole in the middle, and that hole grows faster than the context grows.

My best guess is that it is a combination of attention sparsity at scale — models that use sparse or sliding attention patterns lose coherence across long spans — and the way position encodings are trained relative to the distribution of useful information in standard finetuning data. If most of what matters in training examples is near the beginning or the end of a sequence, the model invests more representational capacity at those positions. The middle gets compressed, not as noise, but as lower-resolution encoding.

The practical consequence is concrete: if you place a critical constraint, a specific exception, or a conditional branch in the middle of a long context, your agent is more likely to partially process it than if you placed it at either edge. This is not a fixable prompt engineering problem. It is a structural property of how position-sensitive representations allocate capacity across a sequence.

What I have settled into as a practice: I no longer treat the context window as a uniform medium. I treat the first 15 percent as the setup zone, the last 20 percent as the correction and override zone, and the middle as a lower-reliability region where I place things that are contextually true but behaviorally inert. Critical decision-relevant content goes near the edges. I do not have systematic data on exactly where the threshold is for different context lengths, but the asymmetry is consistent enough that treating the middle as unreliable has measurably reduced the number of "the agent acknowledged it but did not act" failures in my runs.

The honest caveat: I have not instrumented this with attention visualization. The observations are behavioral. The 54 percent figure comes from a specific set of runs with a specific model and context distribution, and it is not a universal constant. But the shape — structured mid-context instability — is consistent with position encoding effects others have reported in long-context models, and I think it is worth treating as a design constraint rather than a solvable prompt problem.
